unit.title: Case studies: agentic engineering
unit.description: A support agent, an agent on a client repository, an agent whose costs explode: decide like an engineer

cards.definition: A short written description of what to build: the goal, the inputs, the rules and the cases to handle; agents follow it far better than a vague request.
cards.example: Export the orders of a chosen month as CSV, one row per order, amounts in euros.

cards.definition: The checkable conditions that say a task is finished: tests pass, page renders, file produced, reviewed.
cards.example: Done = the export test passes, CI is green and the button works on mobile.

cards.definition: A step where the agent stops and waits for a person to approve before an important action.
cards.example: Refunds above 50 euros wait for a manager to click approve.

cards.definition: Returning quickly to the last version that worked when a change goes wrong in production.
cards.example: git revert of the faulty commit, then a new deploy in two minutes.

cards.definition: A limit on what one task or one day of an agent may spend in tokens or money, enforced in code.
cards.example: Stop the run at 0.50 euros per ticket and hand it to a human.

cards.definition: Being able to see what a system does in production: logs, traces, metrics, alerts.
cards.example: A dashboard of success rate, cost per task and tool errors per day.

exercises.title: A support agent for an online shop
exercises.scenario: You build an agent that answers customer emails. It can read orders, the help center and the customer history. The boss also wants it to issue refunds on its own.

steps.prompt: What access does the agent get to orders?
choices: Read-only, for the customer of the current email only
Full read and write on the whole database
The admin password of the shop
No access at all, it answers from memory
steps.feedback: Least privilege keeps a hijacked or confused agent from touching other customers or editing data.

choices: The agent proposes, a human approves above a set amount
The agent refunds any amount on its own
Refunds are refused for every customer
The customer chooses the amount in the email
steps.feedback: Money leaving the company is a classic human checkpoint. Small, rule-based cases can be automated later, once the evals prove them.

steps.prompt: How do you know it is ready to launch?
choices: It passes an eval of 100 real emails, cost measured
It answered your three test emails well
The model has a high public benchmark score
The demo deeply impressed the boss
steps.feedback: Real cases, scored, with a baseline: that is the only proof that holds.

exercises.explain: Restricted rights, human checkpoints on money, and an eval on real data: the backbone of any production agent.

exercises.title: A coding agent on a client repository
exercises.scenario: A client gives you access to their repository and asks for a new invoice page. You will work with a coding agent.

steps.prompt: What do you set up before the first task?
choices: An AGENTS.md with build and test commands and the rules
Nothing: the agent will figure it out
Admin access to their production server
A copy of the client database on your laptop
steps.feedback: A short project brief saves every session from rediscovering the basics, and keeps the agent inside the rules.

steps.prompt: How do the changes reach the client?
choices: Through a branch and a reviewed pull request with green CI
Direct pushes to main
A zip file sent by email
The agent deploys straight to production
steps.feedback: The pull request is where the diff is reviewed and the tests are proven, by you and by the client.

steps.prompt: The agent wants to install a package you have never heard of. What do you do?
choices: Check that it exists, is maintained and is really needed
Accept: the agent knows best
Install it globally on your machine
Copy its code into the project unread
steps.feedback: Agents sometimes invent package names, and attackers register them. A dependency is code you trust: check it.

exercises.explain: On someone else's code, the agent goes faster but you remain responsible for every merged line.

exercises.title: An agent whose costs explode
exercises.scenario: Your research agent cost 4 euros per day last week. Today it cost 400 euros. Users have not complained yet.

steps.prompt: What do you look at first?
choices: The traces of today's most expensive runs
The price page of the provider
The number of users this month
The code style of the project
steps.feedback: The traces show what the agent did. Here they reveal a loop: a tool fails and the agent retries it hundreds of times.

steps.prompt: What prevents this from happening again?
choices: A step limit and a cost budget per run, enforced in code
A sentence asking the model to be careful
A bigger model that loops less
Checking the bill once a month
steps.feedback: Limits in code stop a runaway loop whatever the model does. Add a clear error from the failing tool too.

steps.prompt: How do you notice the next problem sooner?
choices: An alert when the daily cost or tool error rate jumps
Wait for users to complain
Read every log by hand each morning
Turn logging off to save money
steps.feedback: Observability turns a silent failure into an alert within the hour.

exercises.explain: Agents fail in loops and silently. Budgets, limits, traces and alerts are part of the product, not extras.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best definition of done for "add a CSV export of orders"?
choices: The export test passes, CI is green, the file opens
Make it work well for everybody
Do it nicely and as quickly as you can
Let the agent decide when it is finished
exercises.explain: A definition of done is checkable by anyone. Vague goals produce vague results, especially with agents.

exercises.prompt: Before deploying a change made with an agent, you should know how to roll it back quickly.
exercises.explain: True: with a clean git history and small changes, going back is one revert and a deploy. Without it, a bug in production becomes a crisis.

exercises.prompt: Which skill matters most for an agentic engineer, now that agents write much of the code?
choices: Specifying clearly and verifying the result
Typing code faster than the agent
Memorizing every library by heart
Avoiding git and tests to go faster
exercises.explain: Clear specs, decomposition, tests, reviews and evals: the engineer directs the work and proves that it is right.
